🎨 Risk Classification Scale

Threshold Effects Level (TEL) & Cumulative Contaminant Units (CCU)

Highest Risk (Score 5 / >15)
Severe zinc & copper accumulation exceeding upper TEL thresholds
Higher Risk (Score 3 / 15)
Elevated load exceeding threshold guidelines
Medium Risk (Score 2 / 9)
Moderate contaminant concentration relative to sediment volume
Lower Risk (Score 1 / 1–8)
Detectable upstream sources with low accumulation likelihood
Lowest Risk (Score 0)
Minimal heavy metal concentration
No Upstream Sources (Score -1)
Catchments with zero roading or urban impervious area

🔬 Model Insights & Contaminant Transport Dynamics

Key observations from the simulation across New Zealand catchments

● Urban Concentration Effects

Urban runoff produces the highest localized risk scores (red / orange) due to dense impervious surfaces (roofs, parking, local drainage). These appear primarily around the Auckland isthmus, Christchurch, Tauranga, and Wellington.

● Highway Corridors vs. Local Roads

State Highways carry high heavy-vehicle traffic resulting in continuous tyre wear (Zinc) and brake wear (Copper) along major corridors like SH1, though rural sediment dilution often mitigates in-stream risk compared to urban nodes.

● Coastal Terminal Accumulation

Terminal reaches and estuarine basins act as long-term depositional sinks. Even modest upstream river loads aggregate at coastal boundaries, causing estuary-level CCU to exceed threshold limits in enclosed harbors.

● Sediment Dilution Factors

The RSS model divides contaminant mass by total upstream sediment load (\(g/t\)). Catchments with high natural sediment yields (e.g. West Coast of South Island) show lower risk scores due to strong dilution.

💡 GIS Integration: The corresponding .shp shapefiles in this folder can be opened directly in QGIS / ArcGIS for detailed spatial queries down to individual nzsegment reach IDs.
